what_is_said: Fair-time riots between rival sects; in 1760 Goshains and Bairagis fought a pitched battle at Hardwar, 1,800 said to have perished.
quote: in 1760 the rival mobs of Goshains and Bairagis fought a pitched battle, in which 1,800 are said to have
notes: The Daśanāmī–Bairāgī battle of the Kumbh of 1760; the study's north/ README mentions it among Daśanāmī notes.

what_is_said: Chief zamindars of Kankhal are a rich Udasi body under a mahant elected by the panchayat; they lend money and own much land in Roorkee tahsil; other akharas at Kankhal include Nirmalas, Nirbanis and Niranjanis.
quote: rich and influential body of Udasi Faqirs presided over § a mahant, who is elected by the panchayat of the breth- ren. Besides their religious duties they carry on a considerable trade in money-lending
notes: Nirmala akhara also named at Kankhal; Niranjani/Nirbani are Daśanāmī akhāṛās beside them.

institution: Gokul Das Udasi; Panchaiti Akhara of Nanakshahi Faqirs
what_is_said: Gokul Das Udasi of Kankhal owns four villages and shares, 3,199 acres, revenue Rs 4,412, next to Bhola Gir Goshain (4,024 acres, Rs 4,818); the Panchaiti Akhara of Nanakshahi Faqirs holds five shares in Jwalapur.
quote: Gokul Das Udasi of. Kankhal is the recorded owner of four villages, and oneshare in Jwalapur and two shares in Manglaur, with an area of 3,199 acres and a demand of Rs, 4,412
notes: Direct same-paragraph comparison with the Daśanāmī Bhola Gir.

what_is_said: In Jwalapur pargana Udasi Faqirs hold 4.6 per cent of the land, Goshains 4.9; the Udasis of Kankhal have four villages and one share paying Rs 4,224.
quote: 4°7, Udasi Faqirs 4°6, Brahmans 4°4 and Sheikhs 4°1 per cent, The largest estate is that of the Rani of Landhaura
notes: Pargana share almost equal to the Goshains'.

what_is_said: Faqirs 13,925: Jogis 9,377 scattered through the district; the rest near Hardwar: 1,738 Goshains, 1,518 Bairagis, 533 Sadhus, besides Sannyasis and Udasis.
quote: as many as 9,377 were described as Jogis, and these are scattered throughout the district ; the rest belong -mainly to the Roorkee tahsil
notes: Mixed count (Jogi, Bairagi, Udasi); census 1901.

institution: Guru Ram Rai temple (Gurudwara of the Udasis)
what_is_said: The most important landed proprietor of the district is Mahant Lachhman Das of the Guru Ram Rai temple: Dehra itself paying nominal revenue Rs 11,289, and many other villages in the Dun and Tehri.
quote: The most important landed proprietor from the statistical point of view is Mahant Lachhman Das of the Guru Ram Rai temple in Dehra, He holds, as the endowment of the temple
notes: The single largest ascetic landholder in this assignment's UP volumes.

place: Dehra, Dhartawala, Mihunwala, Panditwari, Rajpur, Chamansari
what_is_said: The mahant holds six named villages revenue-free; these and the grants to Badrinath, Kedarnath, Bharatji and Gorakhnath (Gorakhpur and Jogiwala villages) were made by the Garhwal Raja or the Gurkhas before British rule.
quote: The mahant of the temple of Guru Ram Raj in Dehra holds free of revenue Dehra Khas, Dhartawala, Mihunwala, Panditwari, Rajpur aud Chamansari.
notes: Also a Nāth grant: "Gorakhpur and Jogiwala to Gorakhnath" (same sentence block).

what_is_said: Gurudwara of the Udasis built 1699; mahant elected from the chelas of the last mahant, formerly guided by the Sikh chiefs; nazarana Rs 500 to Government at installation; Sangat fair 8,000–10,000; Ranjit Singh sent Rs 500 in 1826; temple supported by revenue of villages in the Dun and jagirs in Tehri.
quote: The temple or Gurudwara of the Udasis, the sect of religious ascctics founded by Ram Raj, thuir Guru, was built in 1699

what_is_said: Fateh Sah of Garhwal confirmed several villages for the mahant's retinue and temple and endowed a similar institution of Ram Rai at Srinagar; in 1817 Mahant Har Sewak's claim to the Rajpur canal was disallowed.
quote: Fateh Sah and his sucecssor confirmed the possession of several villages for the support of the mahant’s retinue and the service of the temple
notes: Royal (Garhwal) endowment; cf. the Udasi math at Srinagar in Atkinson (AT11).

what_is_said: The rivalry of Bairagis and Goshains culminated on the last day of the 1760 fair in a pitched battle; the Bairagis were defeated with some 1,800 slain; in 1796 the Goshains were defeated by Sikh pilgrims with 500 dead.
quote: The rivalry of the Bairagis and Goshdins culminated on the last day of the fair in 1760 in a pitched battle, which terminated in the defeat of the former, of whom some eighteen hundred were slain.
notes: Atkinson names the losers (Bairāgīs); Nevill (N001) does not.

what_is_said: Mendicant classes of the division: Bairagis over 13,000; Goshains 15,289, many agricultural; Jogis 39,976.
quote: The mendicant classes are fairly represented by the Bairagis, who number over 13,000 souls; the Goshdins (15,289), many of whom have taken to agricultural pursuits
notes: Jogi figure includes the Jogi caste.

what_is_said: The famous temple of Gorakhnath, recently rebuilt, is in a very flourishing condition; pilgrims' offerings bring a considerable income to the Kanphata Jogis in attendance.
quote: The institution is in a very flourishing condition, and is still the resort of numerous pilgrims and worshippers, whose offerings bring in a considerable income to the Kanphata Jogis in attendance at the temple.
notes: No villages or revenue given for the Gorakhnath math in either Gorakhpur volume.

what_is_said: The chief local place of pilgrimage is the shrine of Gorakhnath (c. 1400); the priests are "Earbored" (Kanphata) Jogis; temple said to have been destroyed under Aurangzeb.
quote: The chief of such shrines pilgrimage, is undoubtedly that dedicated at Gorakhpur to Gorakh- nath, a personage who probably lived no earlier than 1400 A.D,
notes: p. 493: "The priests at St. Gorakhn&th’s are Earbored Jogis."

what_is_said: A celebrated math of Vaishnava Bairagis founded c. 80 years ago, with branches at Ajodhya, Barhalganj and Baikunthpur; the mahant (Pauhari Ji) presides over fairs in Gorakhpur, Saran and Ballia; succession of mahants given; the present mahant has begun to accept gifts of landed property.
quote: The monastery is supported by the offer ngs of worshippers, and the present Mahant has departed frtoja the rule of his predecessors by accepting gifts of landed property.

what_is_said: Barhalganj, confiscated from the rebel Raja of Narharpur after the Mutiny, is now owned by the Mahant of Paikauli and a Maulvi; the mahant manages the Charanpaduka thakurdwara and built a new temple.
quote: the preseut owners are the Mahant of Paikauli and A aulvi Subhan-uliah of Gorakhpur

what_is_said: A large math of Vaishnava Bairagis whose mahant, the Pauhari ji, eats only fruit and wanders through Gorakhpur and Saran; established 52 years; branches at Ajudhia, Barhalganj and Baikunthpur.
quote: The place is remarkable for a large math or monastery occupied by Vaishnava Bairégis,> whose prior or mahant is known as the Panbarij ji.
notes: Earlier state of N014; no land then.

what_is_said: Kabir's tomb at Maghar is kept by a Muslim Julaha family with a revenue-free village and 4 annas a day; beside it the samadh of a Hindu mahant who came c. 1764, whose successor holds a revenue-free village in Gorakhpur; the last custodian Man Das was killed in an affray within Kabir's panth; Safdar Jang set aside several villages for the shrine; Pus fair c. 5,000.
quote: The mahant’s suecces- sor has at least nominal charge of his tomb (samddh). The remuneration is in this case a revenue-free village in the Gorakhpur district, but no daily allowance.
notes: Conflict is internal to the Kabīrpanth.

what_is_said: Kabir's shrine is in Julaha custody with a revenue-free village and 4 annas daily from the Gorakhpur treasury, a grant from Safdar Jang's time; a Hindu mahant whose first predecessor came about 1764 has a second shrine nearby.
quote: There is also a Hindu mahant, whose earliest predecessor camo about 1764 and was buried in a second shrine, standing near that of Kabir
notes: Selection file gives year 1801 in error; Basti DG is 1907.

what_is_said: Village ownership by caste: Goshains own 34 villages, Nanakshahis 20 forming a single estate, Bairagis twelve; Bairagis and Goshains also hold shares in other villages.
quote: Goshains  own  34  villages,  Nanakshahis  20,  which form  a  single  estate,  and  Bairagis  twelve.
notes: Udāsī (Nanakshahi) and Bairāgī holdings set beside the Daśanāmī 34 in one sentence. The Nanakshahi estate is Maswasi's Basantpur (N020).

place: Basantpur estate (parganas Gonda, Paharapur, Nawabganj, Guwarich)
what_is_said: Mahant Har Charan Das of Maswasi, a Nanakshahi faqir and taluqdar, successor of Mahant Gur Narain Das who acquired the property by gift and purchase before annexation; holds villages in Unao, Lucknow, Hardoi, Kheri and Bahraich; Gonda property 22 villages and mahals, 17,215 acres, assessed Rs 19,365.
quote: He  is  a  Hanak- shahi  faqir  and.the  successor  of  Mahant  Gur  Narain  Das,  by  whom the  property  was  acquired  by  gift  and  purchase  shortly  before annexation.
notes: A Nānakshāhī (Udāsī) mahant as Oudh taluqdar; the largest ascetic estate in the Oudh volumes read.

what_is_said: Mahant Har Charan Das of Maswasi is one of the largest landholders of Unao, with 28 villages and three pattis, besides estates in Bahraich, Gonda, Kheri, Lucknow and Hardoi; founded by a Nanakshahi faqir, who acquired the villages largely as zamindars put them under his protection against the chakladars; the minor mahant was educated at Canning College under the Court of Wards.
quote: is one of the largest landholders in the district, owning 28 villages and three pattis in Harha, Purwa, Pariar, Sikandarpur, Asoha and Safipur.
notes: Also named as landholder in Lucknow, Hardoi and Kheri DGs (UP33, UP37, UP38).

what_is_said: Temple rebuilt by Ratan Nath, third in descent from Gorakh Nath; some twenty mahants of Debi Patan have presided over the Kanphata Jogis since; desecrated under Aurangzeb; Chait fair of some 75,000 pilgrims and traders, trade in Nepal ponies; priest takes a fee per animal sacrificed. Land belongs to the Maharaja of Balrampur.
quote: Since  Ratan  Nath  there  have been  some  twenty  mahants  of  Debi  Patan,  who  have  presided over  the  brotherhood  of  Kanphata  Jogis
notes: The village itself (588 acres) belongs to Balrampur, not to the Jogis.

what_is_said: Satnamis (Jagjiwan Das's sect) number 19,786 in Bara Banki, more than anywhere save Bahraich; founder a Rajput zamindar of Kotwa (1682–1761) whose guru was Bishweshwar Puri Goshain; the present Mahant, Jaskaran Das, twelfth-generation descendant, heads a large family holding land and allied to taluqdars; gaddis of both clerical orders at Kotwa; shrine built under Asaf-ud-daula; two large fairs.
figures: 19,786 Satnamis (1901); 1682–1761; 12th generation; sects: Ramanandis 5.5%, Satnamis 2%, Nanakshahis 1.6%, Kabirpanthis 1%
quote: Ho  is  styled  Mahaiit,  and  is  the  head of  a large  family,  many  of  whom  hold  landed  jiropcrty  and  are allicd  to  several  of  the  taluqdar^’  families  by  mariiago.
notes: tradition = other: the Oudh Satnāmīs (Jagjīvan Dās), distinct from the Chhattisgarh Satnāmīs. A Daśanāmī (Puri) is named as Jagjīvan Dās's guru.

what_is_said: The successor to Jagjiwan Das's gaddi is Baba Jaskaran Das, twelfth generation; superior clergy called mahant; a regular mahant is appointed only by the full bench of fourteen mahants; members of the family hold estates and marry into taluqdar families; Jagjiwan Das's preceptor was a Goshain worshipper of Shiva.
quote: A regular Mahant can only be appointed by the full bench of Mahahts (at present said to consist of the fourteen above recorded, exclusive of the Kalu Mahant at Kotwa).
notes: tradition = other (Oudh Satnāmī). Comparison with a Goshain guru in the text.

what_is_said: Jagjiwan Das of Kotwa, whose disciples the Satnamis are the most numerous sectaries in Oudh and who enrolled the diwan Tikait Rai, used his hold on the Lucknow darbar to marry his daughter to Raja Guman Singh of Gonda and to have the Pandes banished.
quote: Jagjiwan Das, a fagir of Kotwa, in Bara Banki zila, held the diwéin under some obligation.
notes: Court influence of a sect founder under Asaf-ud-daula.

institution: Patan throne of the Kanphata Jogis
what_is_said: From Ratan Nath twenty mahants have filled the Patan throne; election not by age; the Kanphata priests worship Bhairava, eat meat and drink spirits; the Gorakhnath Jogis of Gonda are divided into Kanphatas, Janganis, Sewaras and Alakhias.
quote: From Ratan Nath to the present day twenty Mahants have filled the Pdtan throne, and two steps' back carry us to Gorakh Nath.

what_is_said: At the last Kumbh (1906) 60,000 Bairagis and others were in the faqirs' camps, 30,000 in procession; danger of conflict among the Bairagis, Nirbanis against Nirmohis and Digambaris; a quarrel in 1906 needed a squadron of cavalry.
quote: there is always a danger of conflict among the Bairagis, between the Nirbanis on one side and the Nirmohis and Digambaris on the other. A quarrel of this nature occurred in 1906
notes: Conflict among the Vaiṣṇava akhāṛās themselves, not with Gosāins.

institution: Chhota Panchayati Akhara; Bara Panchayati Akhara; Nirmala Pili Kothi
what_is_said: Order of precedence at the Magh Mela: Nirbani Naga Goshains (wealthy, Daraganj), Niranjanis and Junas (bankers), then the Bairagis (wandering, without fixed residence), then the Udasi Chhota Panchayati Akhara with a large monastery in Mutiganj, the Bara Panchayati Akhara in Kydganj (very wealthy bankers), the Nanakshahis of Bandhua Hasanpur (Sultanpur) and the Nirmalas of the Pili Kothi, also bankers.
quote: Then comes the Chhota Panchayati Akhara, a body of Udasis of the Punjab, who have a large monastery in Mutiganj.
notes: Daśanāmī and Udāsī akhāṛās appear here as the same type (urban, wealthy, banking); the Bairāgīs as the poor homeless order.

what_is_said: The Bairagis are all Vaishnavites and wandering mendicants without fixed residence, set against the wealthy Saiva Naga akharas; Ramanujis of Daraganj and Ramanandis of Baba Hari Das's dharmsala are rich Vaishnava communities living on alms.
quote: The Bairagis are all Vaishnavites and are wandering mendicants without any fixed residence. They have three divisions, the Nirbanis, the Nirmohis and the Digambaris
notes: tradition: bairagi_ramanandi (kind comparison). Ramanuji community at Daraganj also named.

institution: Bara Panchayati Akhara; Nirmali Akhara; Chhota Panchayati Akhara; Ramanandi akhara
what_is_said: Principal akharas: the Bara Panchayati (Sikhs reading the Granth, democratic government, lend money and own a good deal of land), Nirmali (Pili Kothi), Chhota Panchayati (Udasi, never married); the Ramanandi akhara of Baba Hari Das (Tyagi Vairagis), supported by alms.
quote: Their name panchayati is derived from the democratic mode of government which obtains amongst them. They lend money and own a good deal of land.
notes: Atkinson lists the Daśanāmī akhāṛās after these.

what_is_said: At the Magh Mela every sect except the Bairagis has permanent houses (monasteries or banking-houses) in Allahabad; the Bairagis' camp was only about 12 acres; disputes among the three rival Bairagi sects caused difficulty.
quote: All of these sects (except the Bairdgis, who are wandering homeless mendicants, though each man may have his own locale) have permanent houses

what_is_said: Mahant Dharam Das of Kydganj owns two villages and 38 mahals in Phulpur assessed at Rs 6,033.
quote: Mahant Dharam Das of Kydganj owris two villages and 38 mahals in Phulpur assessed at Rs. 6,033
notes: Order not stated. Kydganj houses the Udāsī Bara Panchayati akhāṛā and the Rāmānandī dharmsala; "Das" suits either. Not attributed.

what_is_said: Temples of Guru Ram Rai's followers at Dehra and Srinagar and smaller ones served by Udasis; Fateh Sah of Garhwal gave Ram Rai several villages in jagir and endowed a math at Srinagar still held by Udasi fakirs; twice-yearly fairs of Punjab Sikhs; the present Mahant Narayan Das is eighth in descent from Ram Rai.
quote: Fateh Sah, Raja of Garhwal, bestowed several villages in jégir on the Guru and also erected and endowed a math at Srinagar still in the possession of Udasi fakirs of the Sikh sect.

what_is_said: Kanphata Jogis conduct worship in all Bhairava temples not served by Khasiyas, are very numerous in the hills and possess several large establishments; their principal seat is Dhinodhar in Kachh; Saiva Sakti worship is in the hands of Kanphatas or Khasiyas; some 65 Nagraja/Bhairava and 60 Bhairava temples in Garhwal.
figures: c. 125 Bhairava/Nagraja temples in Garhwal; <20 in Kumaon
quote: They are very numerous in these hills gnd possess seve- ral large establishments, They follow the TAntrika ritual
notes: No estates quantified.

what_is_said: The oldest and most honoured temple of Satyanath at Dewalgarh is served by Jogis whose chief has the title of Pir, tied in legend to the founding of the Garhwal (Tihri) dynasty; the Siddh-Bauri temple at Kamera, endowed 1744, is served by Kanphata Jogis.
quote: The service of the temple is now conducted by Jogis and their chief has the title of Pir.
notes: Royal-legitimation legend attached to a Nāth seat.

what_is_said: Vaishnava friars known generically as Bairagis minister at most Vaishnava shrines and festivals and acknowledge the spiritual supremacy of the chief of the Sriranga temple and math near Trichinopoly.
quote: The Vaishnava friars known generically as Bairfgis minister at most of the Vaishnava shrines and festivals and acknowledge the spritual supremacy of the chief of the Sriranga temple and math near Trichinopoly
notes: Atkinson ties the hill Bairāgīs to Śrīraṅgam (Rāmānujīya), not to Rāmānanda. In the same section the Śaṅkara seat of the Daśanāmīs is Joshimath.

what_is_said: Among the few revenue-free grants in the Tarai, Nanakmata belongs to the Sikh shrine there, as does one village in Kilpuri; Chaumahla is the revenue-free property of the Mahant at Nanakmata.
quote: One  of  these  is  Nanakmata,  vhich  belongs  to  the  Sikh shrine  there,  as  does  also  one  village  in  Kilpnri.
notes: The text says "Sikh shrine" and "Mahant", not Udāsī. Udāsī control of Nanakmata is outside knowledge, so the tradition is inferred.

what_is_said: The religious fraternities of the hills fall into Goshains (8,860 in 1872, 2,940 in 1881, 2,050 in the Tarai), Jogis, Bairagis, Udasis, Sadhs and others; 1,726 Jogis in 1872, Kanphata and Binakanphata; Naths do domestic priestly service for Khasiyas and tend Bhairava temples, with eighteen sub-divisions; 233 Bairagis, who serve most Vaishnava temples; Udasis are tied to Dehra and Srinagar; Goshains, Jangams, Bairagis and Naths marry and become cultivators.
quote: The census of 1872 record 1,726 Jogis, chiefly belonging to the Kénphata and Binakénphata sections, and the Naths who, perform domestic priestly service for many classes of Kbasiyas and tend the Bhairava temples.
notes: The same passage gives counts for all the orders. Aghori: "a stray specimen" is occasionally seen.

what_is_said: The Aghorpanthis' regular worship is long suppressed; a few still extort alms; one at Gorakhpur was expelled as a nuisance by the judge (Buchanan); in Buchanan's day their chief lived at Benares and taught Brahmans and Rajputs, and the principal landholders of the district had "a strong hankering after" the doctrine.
quote: But in Buchanan's day its chief, who lived at Benares, gave instruction to many respectable persons including Brahmans and Rajputs; while in this district the principal landholders had “a strong hankering after” its doctrine.
notes: On the facing page Atkinson describes the Atiths (Daśanāmīs) as holding "almost all the temples of Shiva", with maths and gadis (comparison).

what_is_said: Atiths, the backsliding Dasnami majority, hold almost all the temples of Shiva through priors who appoint the pujaris; the Radhaballabhi sages, by contrast, are Rajputs living in akharas under the generic names Bairagi and Vaishnava.
quote: The sages of the Radhaballabhis are mostly Rajputs who have forsworn the world and women; who live in places called arenas (akhdra) ; and themselves bear the generic names of Bairagi and Vaishnava.
notes: tradition: vaishnava_other (Rādhāvallabhī) under the generic name Bairāgī. Comparison row.

what_is_said: The ruined fort of Hariharpur is occupied only by some Aghorpanthi faqirs, who have built a temple and a monastery on the site.
quote: the only occupants being some Aghorpanthi Faqirs, who have built a tem- ple and a monastery on the site
notes: The only Aghorī institution found in the assignment's UP volumes; Benares is excluded.

what_is_said: The Bhikha Shahi sect has a convent in the town, with four domed tombs of its departed spiritual guides.
quote: The Bhikha Shahi sect has a convent here, and from the high road can be seen the four dome-covered tombs of its departed spiritual guides
page: s.v. town entry (c. p. 24 of district section)
notes: A Bhīkhā Sāhib (Bāwrī/Satnāmī-type) panth; the town name is not on the lines read and the page is uncertain.

what_is_said: Of the Vaishnavite sects the strongest are Ramanandis, over 50,000, Kabirpanthis nearly 1,200 and Vallabhacharyas a little over 1,000; the Saivites are mostly returned as Lingaits.
quote: the  strongest are  Ramanandis  with  over  50,000  representatives,  Kabirpanthis with  nearly  1,200  and  Yallabhaeharyas  with  a  little  over  1,000
notes: Lay sect return. The census used "Ramanandi" as a default Vaishnava label (cf. N044).

what_is_said: Ramanandi was the default sect recorded for worshippers of Vishnu who could name no sect; the only other sects in numbers were Nanakshahis 6,153 and Kabirpanthis 4,129.
quote: The only other sects found in any numbers were the followers of Nanak Shah, of whom there were 6,153, and Kabirpanthis, who mustered 4,129 members.
notes: Warns that the "Ramanandi" totals are artefacts of enumeration.

what_is_said: The shrine of the Bairagi saint Mangla is supported by 100 bighas held rent-free in Chitaoli village and surrounded by tombs of former heads of the Bairagi community.
quote: One  hundred  bighoB  of  land  are  held  rent-frei^ ... Chitaoli  village  to  support  this  shrine,  which  is  surrounded  by numerous  tombs  of  former  heads  of  Iho  Bairngi  community
notes: Atkinson (AT04c, p. 754) describes the same site: "under the care of a Bairdgi colony from very ancient times". The quote is joined across a page header.

what_is_said: Goshains and Bairagis together own 3,820 acres in various parts of the district; Bairagis are named as co-proprietors in several villages.
quote: Khattris with 6,768, nearly all of which is in Atrauli; Goshains and Bairagis wdth 3,820, in various parts of the district
notes: Daśanāmī and Bairāgī land is not separated. The selection file dates the volume 1879, but the text is Nevill's 1909 Aligarh.

what_is_said: A colony of Nanakshahi faqirs holds a revenue-free grant of 141 acres at Baksar and land in four other villages, a muafi held since Alamgir II; celibates under a mahant who nominates his successor; recruits from Brahmans, Khattris, Jats, Banias and Kayasths; teaching on the lines of the Granth.
quote: In the village there  is  a colony  of  Nanakshahi  faqirs,  who  hold  a revenue-free  granj;  of  141  acres,  as  well  as  in  four  other  villages of  the  district.
notes: The high-peaked caps suggest Udāsīs.

volume: AT03 Atkinson, Meerut division pt 2, Muzaffarnagar (wbsl.15501)
place: shrine of Piyara Ji / Lal Ji
what_is_said: The affairs of the Gujar saint's shrine are managed by Bairagis, who own two-thirds of the village; the saint's followers are Vaishnavas wearing black necklaces.
quote: The affairs of the shrine are managed by Bairdgis, who own two- thirds of the village, while one-third remains in the possession of Piyéra Ji’s descendants.

what_is_said: Bairagi and Saniasi are generic for renouncers, but specifically a Bairagi is a Vaishnava, most often a Ramanandi (Kabirpanthi, Dadupanthi or Sriananda line), and a Saniasi a Saiva; most Vaishnava Bairagis are vagrants, sometimes living in maths; the Bairagi is the lowest rank of a hierarchy that has partly superseded Brahmans as ghostly advisers.
quote: The majorify of the Vaishnava Bairfgis ave vagrants ; but they are sometimes found dwelling together in monasteries (math).

place: Goli, Waisri, Harsinghpur, Sita Mai, Bhandari, Barana, Matnauli
what_is_said: Nimawat Bairagis of Goli, Waisri and Harsinghpur, Ramanandi Bairagis of Sita Mai and Bhandari, and Radha Ballabhi Bairagis of Barana and Matnauli own a good deal of land; property of the asthals passes to chelas; many Bairagis have married (gharbari) and formed a new caste largely drawn from Jats; the monastic communities are powerful, well conducted, often very wealthy and hospitable.
quote: The monastic communities are powerful, are exceedingly well conducted, often very wealthy, and exercise a great deal of hospitality.
notes: Covers three Vaiṣṇava lines (Nimbārka, Rāmānandī, Rādhāvallabhī) under "Bairagi". The 1919 Karnal DG (PB02, line 7264) repeats it.

institution: Bairagi monastery of Goli and its branch
what_is_said: In 1842 the quit-rent of Goli and Waisri was found assigned at a fixed demand to a Bairagi monastery at Goli and its branch at Waisri; in 1852 the NWP Government directed that they keep it.
quote: In 1842 it was found that the Mandals were enjoying the quit rent of the two villages of Goli and Waisri, which were assigned at a fixed demand to a Bairdg? monastery in the former, and its branch in the latter village.
notes: The text is ambiguous about whether the Mandal Pathans or the monastery enjoy the quit-rent.

what_is_said: Thakurdwaras to Ram/Narain are built by Brahmans or Bairagis, and Brahmans and Bairagis take the offerings; Shivalas, built by Banias, have Gosain or Jogi priests, generally Kanphatas, who take the offerings; no Brahman can take Shiva's offerings.
quote: The priests are Gosdins or Jogts, gene- rally of the kanphate or ear-pierced class, and they take the offerings.
notes: tradition: nath_jogi. A village division of ritual labour: Vaiṣṇava shrines go to Bairāgīs, Śiva shrines to Gosāins or Kānphaṭas.

what_is_said: The district has 299 monasteries (asthals) with 659 resident ascetics and 2,725 acres of land grants; Bairagis are half of them, then Kanphata Sadhs, Sadhs, Gosains and Udasis; the Kanphatas of Bohar, a fine block of buildings four miles east of Rohtak, have an evil character and a disreputable fair.
quote: There are no less than 299 monasteries, called asthals, with 659 resident ascetics, and grants of laud amounting to 2,725 acres attached to them. Byragis form half the number
notes: Mixed-order row. About 150 of the asthals are Bairāgī; the Gosāins rank fourth. Bohar is the Nāth seat (Asthal Bohar).

what_is_said: There are no fewer than eight Bairagi mahants with monasteries across the district; celibate, but the mahants engage in secular business and some are learned in Sanskrit.
quote: There are no less than eight Bairagi mahants, whose monasteries are scattered from one end of the district to the other.
notes: The 1905 Hoshiarpur DG (PB07) repeats it. Dādūpanthī colonies in six villages are described next.

institution: Dera Baba Nanak temple; Tali Sahib
what_is_said: The temple's mahants have been chosen from the Udasis since 1758, appointed by the Bedis until a disputed election in 1857 went to a civil court, after which the mahants considered themselves independent; list of seven mahants 1758–1870; a jagir of Rs 2,602 in perpetuity, 50 sadhs fed daily. The Tali Sahib mahants, also Udasi, had a Sikh-period jagir reduced by the British to Rs 2,500 and then to Rs 1,000 in perpetuity. Under the Sikhs the Bedis held jagirs of Rs 2,00,000.
quote: It had been the custom to select the mahants from a sect of sudhe (fagir) known as Udassi, In 1758 A.D., at the time of the erection of the kacha temple, the Bedfs appointed Sangat Bakhsh, a Udast sadh, as the mahunt of the temple
notes: A conflict over succession: Bedi patrons against the Udāsī mahants, settled in a civil court.

what_is_said: Thamman is the centre, home and depot of the Bairagi faqirs; the Baisakhi fair draws about 60,000; Bairagis touring India return for it and share the large collections from their devotees.
quote: The  Bam  Thamman  fair,  held  in  the  village  of  Thammnn,  the centre  home  and  dep6t  of  the  Bairagiybjfrs.

what_is_said: The Tilla monastery, one of the oldest religious institutions in Northern India, is named in the Ain-i-Akbari; its old jagir of Naugiran village, referred to in a sanad of Akbar, was recently restored after more than forty years' resumption, which followed the late gaddi-nashin's connivance in the murder of a faqir; the head (Pir Sahj Nath) is respected by Muslims and Hindus; branches at Kot Sarang and Makhad, with relations claimed as far as Nepal and Afghanistan as the original Jogi foundation; pilgrimage has declined.
figures: jagir resumed >40 years, restored c. 1900s; sacked c. 1748
quote: The  old  jdgxr  heldi  by  the  Jogis  of  the  village  of  Naugiran  is referred  to  in  a sanad  of  Akbar  as  an  ancient  grant : it  has  recently been  restored  after  over  forty  years’  resumption
notes: The Punjab's chief Nāth seat. The PA17 1883 volume (N058) records the resumption.

what_is_said: The Tilla shrine is tended by a corporation of Jogis under a mahant, held in regard even by Muslims; the old jagir was abolished because the present mahant was accused of murdering his rival for the gaddi; the Jogis hold pasture and wood rights in the 26,000-acre Tilla rakh.
quote: The old jagir attached to this shrine has been abolished since the present Mo- hant was accused of murdering his rival for the “ Gadd.”
notes: An internal succession conflict that cost the order its estate.

place: Jat villages of the uplands; Jassowal
what_is_said: The village dharmsala is endowed with land and usually held by an Udasi who reads the Granth; larger ones form colleges under a mahant with affiliated branches. At the Regular Settlement the incumbent was returned as owner of the land, revenue-free; most sadhs then married, closed the dharmsala and became landed proprietors. The Jassowal alms-house had several hundred acres held revenue-free in perpetuity.
quote: But at the Regular Settle¬ ment the incumbent was in every case returned as owner of the land, which was at the same time exempted from revenue for the period of settlement.
notes: Colonial settlement turned religious trusts into private family estates, the same process the study records for Daśanāmī maths.

what_is_said: The large langar at Jaspal Bangar is kept by a marrying family of Udasi faqirs; its endowments, begun under Muhammad Shah and added to by later rulers, are some 800 acres; the mahant's father died in debt keeping it open in famine. The Heran langar, held by an Udasi ascetic, distributed 8,000 maunds of grain in the 1862 famine.
quote: There is also a large langar at Jaspal Hangar, near Ludhiana, which is kept by Ja«paiB&ng«r a family of tldasi faqirs, whoso custom is also to marry.
notes: The quote keeps an OCR marginal note ("Ja«paiB&ng«r").

place: Charan Kaul (Anandpur); Bahadarpur; Chinighati; Manak; Adamwal; Alampur Kotla
what_is_said: Udasis are prominent in the district: four dhuan (orders), with three well-known shrines (Charan Kaul of the Balihasna Udasis; Bahadarpur and Chinighati of the Phal Sahib line); Nirmalas, celibate Sikh devotees with headquarters in Patiala, have three well-known monasteries in the district and many smaller ones.
quote: There are four separate dhuan or orders among Uddsis. There are three well-known shrines in this district
notes: Nirmala row folded in (tradition udasi covers both).

what_is_said: Udasi faqirs own several fine villages in the west of Dipalpur tahsil, among them Bhuman Shah, whose shrine keeps a langar supported by the incumbent's jagir and by the Kambohs, who regard Bhuman Shah (1687–1756) as their patron saint.
quote: Oddsi fuktrs own several fine villages in the west of the Dipdlpur tahstl. Among them is Bhuman Shah at which there is a shrine of the saint of that name.
notes: The 1900 Montgomery DG (PB16, p. 89) repeats it and adds "He was a Kamboh who entered the udasi order."

what_is_said: Shahpur's Jogis (246) derive from Gorakhnath, whose chief monastery is at Tilla, with an offshoot on Kirana hill; the monastery of Koh Kirana received large grants of land revenue from the Sikhs, part of which were confirmed in perpetuity by the British. Bairagis (260) are Ramanandi or Nimanandi.
quote: The monasteiy of Koh Kirana received large grants of land revenue from the Sikhs in this district, part of which were confirmed in perpetuity by the British Gov- ernment.
notes: The study's Shahpur Daśanāmī count is 146 Sanyasis (1891).

what_is_said: The chief Kanphata monasteries of the region are at Bohar in Rohtak and Nohar in Bikaner, with an offshoot of Bohar at Busan containing a shivala and samadhs of gurus; 12 panths from Gorakhnath's chelas; Jogis are often pujaris of village shivalas.
quote: The chief monasteries of the Kanphatte Jogfs in this part of the country are at Bohur in Rohtak and Nohur near Bahadra in Bikaner.
notes: The study records the Daśanāmī Puri guru at Kharak and the Giri guru at Bilak in the same volume.

what_is_said: Dharmsalas in many villages, each under a mahant with sadh disciples, live on alms, but many have land attached and enjoy revenue-free grants; they are occupied by Udasi faqirs, considered Sikhs though not orthodox. Customary law: the Udasi faqirs of Jullundur are not presumed to have abandoned worldly affairs nor excluded from inheritance (P.R. 29 of 1881).
quote: many dharmsdlas have land attached to them and enjoy revenue-free grants. They are occupied by Udasi Fakirs, who here are considered Sikhs, though not orthodox.
notes: Under Punjab customary law Udāsīs keep their inheritance rights.

institution: shrine of Bhai Bhara (Udasis of Guru Sangat Sahib)
what_is_said: Mahant Jhanda Ram, zaildar of Sura and gaddi-nashin of the shrine of Bhai Bhara, occupied by Udasis of Guru Sangat Sahib, holds a jagir of Rs 800, earned by Bhai Bhara for helping Sardar Baghel Singh in the Sikh rising of Sambat 1816; fifth in succession.
quote: Mohant Jhanda Ram holds a jdgir of Rs. 800 at Sura of which place he is Zaildar.
notes: A jagir earned by military service; the mahant is also a zaildar (a revenue official).

what_is_said: Among the principal revenue grantees of Talagang tahsil is the Pir of Kot Sarang (a Nath), with Rs 715.
quote: The  principal  grantees  are  Sardar  Mehr  Singh, Chhachhi,  etc.,  of  Pachnand,  Rs.  6,629,  and  Pir  IMchi  Nath  of Kot  Sarang,  Rs.  715.
notes: Kot Sarang is a Tilla branch (N057).

what_is_said: In the Punjab the Ramanandi/Nimanandi distinction hardly matters; in parts the Bairagis are a true marrying caste (Sirsa, Karnal, Jind; the agricultural Bairagis owning Dig village in Kaithal), while the celibate asthal monks pass property to chelas; the monastic communities are powerful, well conducted, often very wealthy and hospitable, numerous in Hoshiarpur; Ram Thamman's tank is still a great meeting point; Banda was originally a Bairagi; the Kalladhari mahants of Una are both Bairagis and Nanakpanthis.
quote: The  monastic  communities  of  the  Bairdgis  are  powerful  and  ex- ceedingly well  conducted,  often  very  wealthy,  and  exercise  much hospitality.
notes: Rose calls the Bairāgīs "Sita-padris", worshippers of Sita Ram, as against the "Lal-padri" Saniasis.

what_is_said: The Jogis used to be at deadly feud with the Saniasis; 500 Jogis were once defeated by two or three hundred Saniasis in a fight witnessed by Akbar, who sent ash-smeared soldiers to help the Saniasis.
quote: The Jogis  used  to  be  at  deadly  feud  with  the  Saniasis  and  500  of  the  former were  once  defeated  by  two  or  three  hundred  Saniasis.
notes: The Nāth–Daśanāmī counterpart of the Hardwar 1760 battle (N001, N010). This is the Thanesar fight of 1567 (the place is not named on this page).

institution: Jogi panths; Pir Ratn Nath's dera
what_is_said: The twelve Jogi orders assemble at Tilla; Ratn Nath's disciples are exempt from earrings; the branch of Pir Ratn Nath's dera at Midni in Shahpur is held by Bairag-ke Jogis (Darya-nathi panth).
quote: the  branch  cf  Pir  Ratn  Nath’s  dera  at  Midni  in Shlhpur  is  held  by  Bairdg-ke- Jogis.
notes: Page approximate.

place: Amritsar (Bibiksar akhara); Dera Baba Nanak; Jaspal Bangar
institution: Udasi order (four dhuan; bara and chhota akhara; Bhagat Bhagwan; Sangat Sahib)
what_is_said: The Udasis are the oldest and principal Sikh order: four dhuan from Gurditta's disciples form the bara akhara, Pheru's line the chhota akhara; each subdivision has a full organisation for collecting and spending money under a sri mahant with subordinate mahants; Dera Baba Nanak is in Udasi custody; married mahants lose influence and the dharmsala becomes a private residence, except in families like Jaspal Bangar.
quote: Each  subdivision  of  the  Udasis  has  a complete  organisation  for  collect- ing and  spending  money,  and  is  presided  over  by  a principal  mahant, called  sri  mahant,  with  subordinate  mahants  under  him.
notes: Census strength: Jullundur, Rohtak, Ferozepur (Maclagan).

what_is_said: The Bhagat Bhagwan chapter began when Bhagatgir, a Sanniasi on pilgrimage to Hinglaj, was converted with his followers by Nanak's grandson Dharm Chand; its great akhara is at the Bibiksar tank in Amritsar, with akharas at Patna and Bihar and 370 gaddis in Eastern India; they wear matted hair and ashes like Sanniasis.
quote: Bhagatgfr then  became  Dharm  Chand’s  convert,  as  did  all  his  followers,  nnder the  name  of  Bhagat  Bhagwdn.
notes: In this origin story a Daśanāmī (-gir) band becomes Udāsī. It is the largest Udāsī network quantified in the sources read (370 gaddis).

what_is_said: The Nirmalas, sent by Guru Govind Singh to Benares to learn Sanskrit, keep the kes but wear saffron and study orthodox Hindu scriptures; well-disciplined, each monastery under a guru with a visiting council; almost always celibate and of higher moral reputation than other Punjab orders; principal akhara at Hardwar, foundations at Amritsar.
quote: Their  principal  Akhdra  is  at  Hardwdr,  but they  also  have  foundations  at  Amritsar  and  elsewhere.
notes: tradition: Nirmala, coded udasi for want of a separate code. Cf. the Nirmala akhāṛā at Kankhal (N002) and Allahabad (N028).

volume: RUS2 Russell & Hira Lal vol II (TheTribesAndCastesOfTheCentralProvincesOfIndiaVolII)
what_is_said: Seven Bairagi akharas (Digambari, Khaki, Munjia, Kathia, Nirmohi, Nirbani, Lasgari) meet every twelve years at Allahabad, Nasik, Ujjain or Hardwar; their Naga members carried the standards and fought; quarrels with the Gosains usually occurred at the sacred rivers over which sect should bathe first; the Lasgaris wear three white lines because they were attacked by Gosains before finishing the sect-mark.
quote: The  quarrels  between  the  Bairagis  and  Gosains usually  occurred  at  the  sacred  rivers,  and  the  point  of  con¬ tention  was  which  sect  should  bathe  first.
notes: The Nirbanis "commonly marry and accumulate property". Russell (p. 99) says the seven akharas "were instituted when the Bairagis had to fight with the Gosains".

volume: RUS2 Russell & Hira Lal vol II (TheTribesAndCastesOfTheCentralProvincesOfIndiaVolII)
institution: Bairagi maths; Nandgaon and Chhuikhadan States
what_is_said: Bairagis numbered 38,000 in 1911 and have become a caste; maths usually have some small land endowment, and a married mahant's headship may pass in his family; many Bairagis have become landholders and moneylenders; two who acquired zamindari land in Chhattisgarh for loans to Gond zamindars, and were given zamindari status by the Marathas, were made Feudatory Chiefs of Nandgaon and Chhuikhadan, now succeeding by primogeniture.
quote: Two  such  men  who  had  acquired  possession^oT extensive  tracts  of  zamindari  land  in  Chhattlsgarh,  in  satis¬ faction  of  loans  made  to  the  Gond  zamlndars,  and  had  been given  the  zamindari  status  by  the  Marathas,  were  subse¬ quently  made  Feudatory  Chiefs  of  the  Nandgaon  and Chhuikhadan  States.
notes: The only Feudatory States in the assignment held by an ascetic order. The CP README states that the Gosāins had none.

volume: RUS3 Russell & Hira Lal vol III (russell_vol3_gutenberg)
what_is_said: Gosains and Bairagis often quarrelled over the merits of Siva and Vishnu, above all over the right to bathe first in the Ganges at Allahabad or Hardwar: the Gosains claim it because the Ganges flows from Siva's locks, the Bairagis because it rises from Vishnu's foot; in 1760 a pitched battle ended in the defeat of the Bairagis with 1,800 slain.
quote: In 1760 a pitched battle on this question ended in the defeat of the Bairagis, of whom 1800 were slain.
notes: tradition: bairagi_ramanandi. Russell copies Atkinson (N010) and adds the theological reason for the precedence dispute.

volume: RUS1 Russell & Hira Lal vol I (in.ernet.dli.2015.211519)
place: Kawardha; Damakheda (near Simga, Raipur); Kudarmal (Bilaspur); Mandla
what_is_said: The two headquarters of the sect are Benares (Kabirchaura Math, "Bap") and Kawardha/Damakheda (Dharam Das Math, "Mai"), independent of each other; 500,000 of India's 850,000 Kabirpanthis (1901) were in the CP; the Kawardha mahants descend from Dharam Das, a Kasaundhan Bania, promised 42 generations; Ugranam (born of a Marar woman) lost a Bombay High Court case to Dhirajnam, who holds the Kawardha seat, but Ugranam at Damakheda has the people's homage; subordinate mahants buy letters of jurisdiction and keep the offerings, two-thirds of them married; a celibate dissenting branch (Nadiapanthi) in Raipur.
quote: at Benares and at Kawardha, the capital of the State of that name, or Damakheda in the Raipur District.
notes: A succession dispute settled in court (Bombay High Court). The gaddī holds jurisdiction over followers, not land.

what_is_said: The mahant's headquarters are at Kawardha, formerly attached to Bilaspur, and the principal fair at Kudarmal; the rival mahants Dhirajnam (official, at Kawardha) and Ugranam (the people's mahant, at Kudarmal) went to the Bombay High Court; the weaving and lower castes (Pankas, Koris, Telis, Chamars) are Kabirpanthis; nearly half a million in the Province in 1901, 99,260 in Bilaspur.
quote: The  total  number  of  Kabirpanthis ‘returned  in  the  Province  in  1901  was  nearly  half  a million, of  whom  99,260  were  residents  of  Bilaspur.
notes: Ugranam's residence is given as Kudarmal here and as Damakheda in Russell.

what_is_said: The Lormi tahutdari of 104 villages (94 sq. miles) was given in charity to Baramdas Bairagi by the Raja of Nagpur in 1826; his chela Lakhmidas succeeded in 1853; it is now divided among Lakhmidas's four sons (two wives), the eldest recognised as head; after their partition quarrel the estate was attached for revenue default.
quote: It  is  said  that  the  taluk  was  originally  given  in  charity  to  one  Baramdas  Bai- ragi in  1826  by  the  Raja  of  Nagpur.
notes: A Maratha grant passing from chela succession to sons by birth. Grant 1870 (N083) gives 103 villages and 58,368 acres.

what_is_said: Mahant Gautamdas, twelfth successor of the Nihang (celibate) Bairagi gaddi of Seorinarayan, has a math with 6 revenue-free villages, said to be granted by the Raja of Ratanpur, and 12 ordinary villages acquired in 1858; his predecessor Arjundas held the gaddi 44 years and built tanks, wells and schools; certificate of loyalty 1877.
quote: To  this  math  Bve  attached  6 revenue-free  and  I2  ordinary villages.  The  former  are  said  to  have  been  granted  by  the Raja  of  Ratanpur
notes: A celibate line set against Lormi's married one.

what_is_said: About 10,000 Bairagis and Gosains in the district hold proprietary rights in many villages; the Lormi family are Bairagis and in Raipur several Gosain families hold large estates; such estates began with temple mahants investing surplus offerings in land or moneylending; Nandgaon and Chhuikhadan were obtained the same way. At settlement Bairagis owned 156 of 2,242 villages.
figures: c. 10,000 Bairagis + Gosains; Bairagis 156 of 2,242 villages
quote: Besides  the  estates  in  Raipur  and  Bilaspur,  the Feudatory  States  of  Nandgaon  and  Chhuikiiadan  belong  to Hairfigi  families  and  were  obtained  in  the  same  manner.
notes: One model of estate formation for both orders.

what_is_said: Bajrangdas, Mahant of Raipur, a Bairagi, owns about 30 villages, mostly muafi, for the upkeep of the Dudhadhari temple, and once had a lakh of khandis of grain in store; listed straight after the Gosain Dharampuri, who holds 40 villages, his akhara gone.
quote: Bajrangdas  Mahant  of  Raipur  is a Bairagi.  He  owns  about  30  villages  mostly  muafi  for  the maintenance  of  the  Dudhadhari  temple  at  Raipur.
notes: Bairāgī and Daśanāmī estates of similar size in one paragraph.

what_is_said: Lormi, a taluka of 103 villages, 58,368 acres (92 sq. miles), population 20,320, is a valuable property owned by a Bairagi, to whose father it was granted some forty years ago.
quote: This is a valuable property, and is^owned by a Bairdgi, to whose father it was granted some forty years ago.

what_is_said: Raipur is the Satnami headquarters, the chief guru living at Bhandar; 389,599 Satnamis in the Province (1901), 224,779 in Chhattisgarh, about 52% of the Chamars; Ghasi Das's grandsons Ajab Das and Agarman Das partitioned their 4–5 villages, became rivals, and through extravagance lost them; Bhandar has passed to the firm of Raja Gokuldas.
quote: Formerly  joint,  they  afterwards  partitioned  their  estate consisting  of  4  or  5  villages.  Their  separation,  however, brought  them  into  rivalry  and  their  consequent  extravagance led  to  the  loss  of  their  villages.
notes: tradition other: the Chhattisgarh Satnāmīs, a Chamar sect. The Kabīrpanthī "Guru Ghasi Das" samādhi on p. 265 is another man (cf. N086).

volume: RUS1 Russell & Hira Lal vol I (in.ernet.dli.2015.211519)
what_is_said: Ghasi Das (d. 1850) left over a quarter of a million disciples; his son Balak Das outraged Hindus by assuming the sacred thread and was assassinated by Rajputs in 1860; a bitter antagonism between Chamars and Hindus has produced riots and murders, and but for British power the movement might have become a social war.
quote: He  was  succeeded  in  the  office  of  high priest  by  his  eldest  son  Balak  Das.  This  man  soon  outraged the  feelings  of  the  Hindus  by  assuming  the  sacred  thread
notes: A conflict with the caste order, not with the Daśanāmīs. Russell derives the creed from Jagjīvan Dās (cf. N023).

what_is_said: In the village is a monument to one Ghasi Das, a saint of the Kabirpanthis; a representative from Kawardha, headquarters of the Kabirpanthis, lives there to tend it and receive offerings. Bhandar is the Satnami sanctuary, its temple-house visited three times a year for confession and absolution.
quote: the centre of the village is a chabdtrd, or Vom monument to one Ghdsi Dds, a saint among theKabir Panthis.
notes: The village name is not on the lines read.

what_is_said: Both claimants to the gaddi have left Kawardha: Ugranam is at Kudarmal (Bilaspur), Dhirajnam at Damakhera (Raipur); hereditary lieutenants with fixed gaddis have become independent through the quarrels of the two mahants, so that in Jubbulpore followers do not know who the Kawardha mahants are and recognise local mahants; an itinerant order converts many low-caste Hindus each year.
quote: These  have  in  many  cases  become  independ- ent  owing  to  the  quarrels  of  the  two  Mahants  at  the  parent gaddl .
notes: Its placement of the two claimants is the reverse of Russell's (N077) and Bilaspur's (N078). The split dissolved central authority.

what_is_said: The village of Bichhia Kap was granted to Ramdas Bairagi by the Nagpur Government in 1799 for the temple of Thakurji.
quote: the  village  Bichhia  Kap granted  to  Ramdas  Bairagi  by  the  Nagpur  Government  in 1799  A.D.  for  the  temple  of  Thakurji
notes: A Bhonsla grant to a Bairāgī. The study records the Bhonsla grant of Bheraghat to a Gosāin in the same district.

what_is_said: The Ramchandra temple, built c. 200 years ago by Bhagwandas Maharaj Bairagi and now managed by Ramanujdas Bairagi, has a jagir producing Rs 1,100, from which wandering Bairagis must be entertained and given dakshina.
quote: of Ramanujdas Bairagi, whose chelas ivorship the images. A ‘jdglr producing Rs. 1100 is attached to the temple,
notes: Berar. The study's Berar Gosāins are village priests under Mahur.

volume: CP08 file dli.ministry.07867 (labelled Nimar; text is Balaghat DG)
what_is_said: 17,038 Kabirpanthis in the district, mostly near Kawardha where one head of the sect lives, chiefly Pankas and Marars; wandering priests in white head-dresses collect offerings and local Kabirpanthis visit their guru at Kawardha.
quote: There are 17,038 Kabirpanthis in the District, mostly in the parts bordering on Kawardhi, where one of the heads of the sect lives
notes: The selection file labels this identifier Nimar, but the running heads read BALAGHAT.

what_is_said: Bham, Raghuji Bhonsla's residence as sirdeshmukh of Berar, is said to have had 5,000 houses of Bairagis besides other followers.
quote: It is said that there were 5000 houses of Bairagis besides great numbers of other followers with him.
notes: Tradition only. Bairāgīs in Bhonsla service; the study notes Bhonsla use of Gosāin Nāgās in Raipur.

volume: RUS2 Russell & Hira Lal vol II (TheTribesAndCastesOfTheCentralProvincesOfIndiaVolII)
what_is_said: Quoting Fuller, about ten thousand persons classed themselves as Aghoris at census time, not all practising cannibalism; the article is otherwise anecdotes of corpse-eating (Rewah, Patiala 1898).
quote: There  are  actually ten  thousand  persons  who  at  census  time  classed  them¬ selves  as  Aghoris.
notes: All-India figure, not CP. No Aghorī institution in the CP sources.

what_is_said: Nandgaon, a feudatory chiefship attached to Raipur, has 560 villages in four parganas; the chief is a Bairagi, and because the sect is celibate succession has been by adoption; the grantee was the family priest of the Raja of Nagpur, the grant dates from 1723 with additions in 1765 and 1818; annual tribute nearly Rs 46,000.
quote: The chief is by caste a Bairdgf, or religious devotee, and celibacy ’being' one of the observances of the sect, the succession has been maintained by adoption.
notes: The largest ascetic-held territory in the assignment. Grant's account (a priestly grant, adoption) differs from Russell's (N075: loans to Gond zamindars, then primogeniture by 1916). The Chhuikhadan entry (p. 170) is illegible in the OCR apart from "A.D. 1750".

what_is_said: In Bilaspur, Kurmis, Rajputs, Bairagis, Banias and Chamars hold about equal numbers of villages; the Bairagi share is swelled by Lormi (103 villages); two or three other Bairagis and Banias hold several villages obtained as grants for cultivation under the Native government.
quote: The proportion of Bairdgi and Baniil villages is swelled by tho fact of a tdluka, in each mst^ce, being held by a member of this caste, fqr Lormf, containing 103 villages, is held by a Bairdgi

what_is_said: Principal proprietary castes in the malguzari area: Brahmans 353 villages, Kurmis 303, Telis 175 … Gonds 61, Bairagis 41, Muhammadans 40.
quote: the Kurmis 303, the Telis 175, the Rajputs 159, the Banias 159, Chamars 69, Marathas 67, Lodhis 66, Gonds 61, Bairagis 41, Muhainmadans 40, Koshtas 36
notes: Drug has a Gosāin malguzar (Ramsahaigir of Maro, p. 65) but no Gosāin village total.
